Definition

Obesity is excessive adiposity with adverse health effects. WHO defines it as BMI ≥30 kg/m² (overweight: 25–29.9; central obesity in Asians: waist >90 cm men, >80 cm women).

Etiopathogenesis

  • Positive energy balance — caloric intake > expenditure (sedentary lifestyle, energy-dense diet).
  • Genetic — monogenic obesity (leptin, leptin-receptor, POMC, MC4R mutations); polygenic ("common obesity").
  • Neuroendocrine — hyperactivity of orexigenic NPY/AgRP neurons; hypoactivity of anorexigenic POMC/CART neurons; ghrelin ↑, leptin & insulin resistance.
  • Endocrine — hypothyroidism, Cushing syndrome, PCOS, growth hormone deficiency, hypogonadism.
  • Drugs — antipsychotics (olanzapine, clozapine), steroids, tricyclics, insulin, sulfonylureas, β-blockers, gabapentin, pizotifen.
  • Gut microbiome — increased Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio enhances calorie harvest.
  • Early life — maternal obesity, gestational diabetes, low birth weight followed by rapid catch-up growth.
  • Psychosocial — stress (cortisol), sleep deprivation, depression.

Sequelae (Complications)

  1. Metabolic — insulin resistance, type-2 diabetes, metabolic syndrome, NAFLD / NASH, dyslipidaemia, gout, cholelithiasis.
  2. Cardiovascular — hypertension, atherosclerosis, coronary disease, heart failure, stroke, venous thromboembolism, varicose veins.
  3. Respiratory — obstructive sleep apnoea, obesity-hypoventilation syndrome (Pickwickian), asthma exacerbation.
  4. Musculoskeletal — osteoarthritis (knees, hips), gout, low back pain, disability.
  5. Endocrine / reproductive — PCOS, infertility, erectile dysfunction, pregnancy complications (pre-eclampsia, GDM).
  6. GI — GERD, gallstones, NAFLD, colorectal & pancreatic cancer.
  7. Oncologic — increased risk of breast, endometrial, colon, renal, oesophageal, pancreatic, liver cancers.
  8. Psychosocial — depression, anxiety, social stigma.
  9. Skin — acanthosis nigricans, intertrigo, striae, lymphoedema.

Clinical Pearl

Central (visceral) adiposity is more dangerous than subcutaneous — it releases free fatty acids & pro-inflammatory adipokines (TNF-α, IL-6, leptin, resistin) and reduces adiponectin, driving insulin resistance and atherogenesis. Waist circumference and waist-hip ratio are better predictors of metabolic risk than BMI alone.

Definition

Carcinogenesis is the multistep process by which normal cells are transformed into malignant cells through accumulation of genetic and epigenetic alterations in oncogenes, tumour-suppressor genes and DNA-repair genes — producing the hallmarks of cancer: self-sufficiency in growth signals, evasion of apoptosis, limitless replicative potential, sustained angiogenesis, tissue invasion & metastasis, and genomic instability.

Viral Carcinogenesis

Oncogenic viruses contribute to ~15–20% of human cancers globally. They act by integrating viral DNA into the host genome (or persisting as episomes), expressing viral oncoproteins that drive proliferation and disable tumour-suppressor pathways, or by inducing chronic inflammation and immunosuppression.

Three vaccines already reduce viral cancer burden: HPV vaccine (cervical & oropharyngeal cancer), HBV vaccine (hepatocellular carcinoma), and HCV antiviral cure (DAAs). Prevention is currently the most powerful tool against virus-induced cancers.

Diagnostic Criteria for SLE

Two systems are widely used — the SLICC 2012 (Systemic Lupus International Collaborating Clinics) and the newer EULAR/ACR 2019. ANA is the entry criterion in both.

SLICC 2012 — ≥4 criteria (at least 1 clinical + 1 immunological)

Clinical (11):

  • Acute cutaneous lupus (malar rash, photosensitive, subacute cutaneous)
  • Chronic cutaneous lupus (discoid, panniculitis, lupus tumidus)
  • Nonscarring alopecia
  • Oral / nasal ulcers
  • Joint disease — synovitis involving ≥2 joints
  • Serositis — pleurisy or pericarditis
  • Renal — urine protein >500 mg/24 h or RBC casts
  • Neurologic — seizures, psychosis, mononeuritis, myelitis, peripheral neuropathy, acute confusional state
  • Haemolytic anaemia
  • Leukopenia (<4000) / lymphopenia (<1000)
  • Thrombocytopenia (<100,000)

Immunological (6): ANA above lab reference range; anti-dsDNA; anti-Sm; antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2-glycoprotein I); low complement (C3, C4, CH50); direct Coombs test (in absence of haemolytic anaemia).

EULAR/ACR 2019

ANA ≥1:80 (entry). Additive weighted score ≥10 from clinical domains (constitutional, haematologic, neuropsychiatric, mucocutaneous, serosal, musculoskeletal, renal) and immunological domains (SLE-specific antibodies, antiphospholipid, complement). Renal biopsy class III/IV/V lupus nephritis earns 8 & 10 points respectively. Sensitivity ~92%, specificity ~93%.

Clinical Pearl

ANA is the screening test; anti-dsDNA & anti-Sm are highly specific (>95%) and confirm SLE. Anti-dsDNA titres also track disease activity and correlate with lupus nephritis. Low complement (C3, C4) suggests active immune-complex disease.

Indications for CSF Examination

  • Suspected meningitis (pyogenic, tuberculous, viral, fungal) or encephalitis
  • Subarachnoid haemorrhage (if CT negative but clinical suspicion high — xanthochromia)
  • Demyelinating disorders — multiple sclerosis, Guillain-Barré, transverse myelitis (oligoclonal bands)
  • CNS syphilis, neuroborreliosis, neurocysticercosis, cryptococcal meningitis (HIV)
  • CNS malignancy — carcinomatous meningitis, leukaemia/lymphoma (cytology)
  • Demarcation of treatment response in tuberculous or pyogenic meningitis
  • Measurement of intracranial pressure (idiopathic intracranial hypertension, normal-pressure hydrocephalus)
  • Therapeutic — intrathecal methotrexate, baclofen pump

Contraindications

  • Raised intracranial pressure (esp. with posterior fossa lesion) — risk of tonsillar herniation; perform fundoscopy & CT/MRI first.
  • Bleeding diathesis — platelets <50,000, INR >1.5, on anticoagulants (correct first).
  • Local skin infection at the puncture site (cellulitis, abscess).
  • Suspected spinal cord compression / epidural abscess — image first.
  • Severe scoliosis / spina bifida — relative; image-guided approach.
  • Uncooperative / combative patient — sedation needed.
  • Cardiorespiratory compromise (cannot tolerate lateral decubitus posture).

Complications

  • Post-lumbar puncture headache — commonest (10–30%); due to CSF leak through dural puncture. Reduced by smaller needle (25 G), bevel parallel to dural fibres, hydration, supine rest 1–2 h; treat with caffeine, epidural blood patch if persistent.
  • Back pain at the puncture site — local trauma, transient.
  • Herniation — rare but fatal, in raised ICP.
  • Infection — iatrogenic meningitis, epidural abscess, discitis.
  • Bleeding — spinal epidural/subdural haematoma (especially coagulopathic).
  • Rare — 6th nerve palsy, intracranial subdural haematoma, pneumocoelous, neurogenic bladder.

Clinical Pearl

Always look at the fundus for papilloedema and obtain a CT/MRI brain in immunocompromised, focal neurology, seizures, altered sensorium or HIV-positive patients before lumbar puncture. Opening pressure, cell count, glucose, protein, gram stain, AFB, culture and viral PCR are the minimum dataset to interpret CSF.

Definition

Exfoliative cytology is the microscopic examination of cells that are spontaneously shed (desquamated) or mechanically scraped/brushed from body surfaces — used as a rapid, minimally invasive screening and diagnostic tool.

Sample Types

  • Naturally shed — sputum, urine, CSF, pleural, pericardial & peritoneal fluids, nipple discharge.
  • Scraped / brushed — Pap smear (cervix), buccal smear, lesion scrapings; brushings during endoscopy/bronchoscopy; cervical, oesophageal, gastric, biliary, bronchial brush cytology.
  • Fluid after centrifugation — body cavity effusions.

Procedure (Pap smear)

  1. Patient in lithotomy; speculum inserted without lubricant (saline only).
  2. Sample transformation zone with Ayre's spatula + endocervical brush (or liquid-based cytology with broom-type device).
  3. Smear on slide & fix immediately in 95% ethanol (conventional) OR rinse into liquid medium (ThinPrep, SurePath).
  4. Stain with Papanicolaou stain (haematoxylin, Orange G, EA polychrome); air dry & mount.
  5. Report using Bethesda system — NILM, ASC-US, ASC-H, LSIL, HSIL, SCC, AIS, glandular cell atypia.

Advantages

  • Simple, cheap, OPD-based, painless, repeatable.
  • High sensitivity for premalignant lesions (Pap smear has reduced cervical cancer mortality by >70%).
  • Liquid-based cytology improves sample quality & allows HPV DNA co-testing.

Limitations

  • Requires expert cytopathologist — inter-observer variability.
  • False negatives — poor sampling, inflammation, blood, scant dyskaryotic cells.
  • Cannot assess invasion depth — biopsy needed for confirmation.
  • Less sensitive for high post-menopausal squamocolumnar junction (use endocervical brush).

Clinical Pearl

The single most cost-effective cancer screening test ever devised is the cervical Pap smear. Combined with HPV DNA testing, sensitivity for high-grade CIN exceeds 95%. All women 21–65 years should be screened every 3 years (or every 5 years with HPV co-testing 30+).

Physical Examination of Urine

  1. Colour
    • Pale yellow — dilute (polyuria, diabetes insipidus)
    • Dark yellow — concentrated (dehydration, fever, jaundice first morning sample)
    • Red / brown — haematuria, haemoglobinuria, myoglobinuria, porphyria, beetroot, rifampicin, phenytoin
    • Black on standing — alkaptonuria, melanuria
    • Green-blue — pseudomonas, methylene blue, amitriptyline, propofol
    • Milky — chyluria, pyuria, phosphaturia
  2. Appearance / Transparency — clear (normal); cloudy (pyuria, phosphate crystals in alkaline urine, amorphous urates, chyluria, spermatozoa); frothy (proteinuria).
  3. Odour — aromatic (normal); ammoniacal (UTI, stale); faecal (colo-vesical fistula); fruity (ketones, DKA); mousy (phenylketonuria); cabbage/maple syrup (MSUD); sweaty feet (isovaleric acidaemia).
  4. Foam test — persistent yellowish foam = proteinuria; red foam = haematuria.
  5. Volume — 24-h urine 600–1800 mL. Polyuria >3 L/d; oliguria <400 mL/d; anuria <100 mL/d.
  6. Specific gravity — 1.003–1.030. Low (1.001–1.005) in diabetes insipidus, over-hydration. High (>1.025) in dehydration, glycosuria, proteinuria. Fixed at 1.010 in chronic renal failure.
  7. pH — 4.5–8.0 (average 6.0). Acidic in high-protein diet, DKA, lactic acidosis, diarrhoea, NH4Cl. Alkaline in vegetarian diet, UTI with urea-splitting organisms (Proteus, Klebsiella), vomiting, renal tubular acidosis, diuretics.
  8. Deposits — phosphates (white, alkaline), urates (pink, acidic), oxalates (envelope-shaped), blood clots, gravel.

Clinical Pearl

Dark urine + tea-coloured froth + positive blood on dipstick but no RBCs on microscopy = haemoglobinuria / myoglobinuria (rhabdomyolysis, intravascular haemolysis). Always confirm with serum CK / LDH / haptoglobin and plasma-free haemoglobin.

Laboratory Investigations in Diabetes Mellitus

  1. Fasting plasma glucose (FPG) — ≥126 mg/dL after 8 h fast (normal <100; prediabetes 100–125).
  2. 2-h post-prandial / OGTT plasma glucose — ≥200 mg/dL after 75 g glucose load.
  3. Random plasma glucose — ≥200 mg/dL with classical symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss) diagnostic.
  4. HbA1c (glycated haemoglobin) — ≥6.5% diagnostic; 5.7–6.4% prediabetes; reflects glycaemic control over preceding 8–12 weeks.
  5. Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) — 75 g glucose; sample at 0, 30, 60, 90, 120 min; diagnose gestational DM (75 g, IADPSG criteria) and borderline diabetes.
  6. Urine glucose — appears when blood glucose exceeds renal threshold (~180 mg/dL).
  7. Urine & blood ketones — β-hydroxybutyrate (preferred), AcAc; diagnosing DKA.
  8. C-peptide — distinguishes type-1 (low) from type-2 (high/normal); evaluates residual β-cell function.
  9. Islet autoantibodies — anti-GAD65, IAA, IA-2, ZnT8 — confirm type-1 diabetes in adults.
  10. Insulin level — high in insulin resistance (type-2, insulinoma); low in type-1.
  11. Lipid profile — high TG, low HDL, small dense LDL; cardiovascular risk.
  12. Renal function & urine microalbumin — ACR >30 mg/g = diabetic nephropathy.
  13. Fundus examination — retinopathy screening at diagnosis of type-2 DM and yearly thereafter.
  14. Foot examination — monofilament, vibration perception, ABI.

HbA1c is unreliable in pregnancy, haemolytic anaemia, recent transfusion, haemoglobinopathies and uraemia. For gestational diabetes mellitus screening, use 75 g OGTT at 24–28 weeks — one elevated value (fasting ≥92, 1-h ≥180, 2-h ≥153 mg/dL) diagnoses GDM (IADPSG).

Laboratory Diagnosis of HIV/AIDS

  1. Screening — 4th-generation combo ELISA/CIA — detects HIV-1 p24 antigen + HIV-1/2 antibodies; window period ~2–3 weeks. 5th-generation also distinguishes p24 from antibody.
  2. Confirmatory — HIV-1/2 differentiation immunoassay (e.g. Geenius) or Western blot. Distinguishes HIV-1 vs HIV-2.
  3. Nucleic acid tests (NAT)
    • HIV-1 RNA PCR (viral load) — diagnosis in window period, neonates (maternal antibody confounds), elite controllers, and treatment monitoring. <20 copies/mL is undetectable.
    • HIV-1 DNA PCR — for early infant diagnosis (<18 mo).
  4. Rapid tests — immunochromatographic finger-prick whole-blood / oral fluid; useful in voluntary counselling, OPD, labour ward. Three-test algorithm in India (NACO).
  5. Baseline staging
    • CD4+ T-lymphocyte count — normal >500; AIDS if <200; initiate ART if <350 or any AIDS-defining illness.
    • Plasma HIV-1 RNA viral load — baseline and at 2–8 wks, then every 3–6 months.
  6. Resistance testing — genotype (commonest) before starting ART and on virological failure; phenotype if complex.
  7. Co-infection & OI screening — HBsAg, anti-HCV, VDRL, TST/IGRA, CD4, toxoplasma serology, cryptococcal antigen (if CD4 <100), Pap smear, chest X-ray.
  8. Other baseline tests — CBC, LFT, KFT, fasting lipid profile & glucose, urinalysis, G6PD (before dapsone/sulfa), pregnancy test.

Clinical Pearl

In infants <18 months, maternal antibodies cross placenta — serology is unreliable. Use HIV-1 DNA PCR (or RNA) at 6 weeks (NACO), repeat at 6 months & 12 months. A positive result requires confirmation on a second sample before starting ART.

Stages of Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)

The Westergren ESR measures the distance (in mm) that red cells fall in a vertical anticoagulated column over 1 hour. Three distinct phases occur:

  1. Stage of aggregation / rouleaux formation (0–10 min)
    • Red cells aggregate face-to-face forming rouleaux (coin-stack appearance).
    • Driven by plasma acute-phase proteins (fibrinogen, IgG, IgM, α2-macroglobulin, haptoglobin, CRP) which neutralise the negative zeta potential (sialic acid) on RBC surface.
    • Aggregates are heavier than individual cells and sediment faster.
  2. Stage of settling / sedimentation (10–40 min)
    • Rouleaux stacks fall under gravity at near-constant velocity; this is the linear phase that determines the 1-hour reading.
    • Sedimentation velocity follows Stokes' law: v ∝ r²; hence large aggregates settle fastest.
  3. Stage of packing (40–60 min)
    • Aggregates accumulate at the bottom and pack tightly; rate slows as cells reach the floor of the tube.
    • Final height of packed cell column at 1 h = ESR (mm/h).

Reference Ranges (Westergren)

  • Adult men: 0–15 mm/h
  • Adult women: 0–20 mm/h
  • Children: 0–10 mm/h
  • Elderly: up to ~30 (men) / ~35 (women)

Clinical Pearl

ESR reflects plasma viscosity and acute-phase reactants. CRP rises and falls faster (hours vs days) and is therefore preferred for monitoring acute inflammation. Markedly raised ESR (>100 mm/h) suggests multiple myeloma, polymyalgia rheumatica, temporal arteritis, malignancy or chronic infection (TB, endocarditis).

Causes of Increased ESR

  • Infections — pyogenic (pneumonia, abscess), TB, subacute infective endocarditis, osteomyelitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, HIV.
  • Inflammation / autoimmune — rheumatoid arthritis, SLE, polymyalgia rheumatica, giant-cell arteritis, vasculitis, inflammatory bowel disease.
  • Malignancy — multiple myeloma (often >100), lymphoma, leukaemia, carcinoma (especially with metastases), Waldenström macroglobulinaemia.
  • Tissue necrosis — MI, malignancy, surgery, trauma, infarction.
  • Pregnancy & menstruation — physiological rise; third trimester ESR may exceed 40 mm/h.
  • Drugs — OCPs, oestrogens, methyldopa, penicillamine, dextran, vitamin A.
  • Endocrine — hyperthyroidism, hypothyroidism.
  • Chronic renal failure / nephrotic syndrome — ↑ fibrinogen, ↑ globulins.
  • Anaemia — reduced haematocrit increases rouleaux.
  • Other — old age, female sex, obesity, smoking, recent vaccination.

Causes of Decreased ESR

  • Polycythaemia — Vera, secondary (hypoxia, tumour).
  • Severe leucocytosis (>50,000) — viscosity overshoots.
  • Abnormal RBC shape — sickle cell disease, spherocytosis, acanthocytosis, poikilocytosis (cannot form rouleaux).
  • Plasma protein abnormalities — hypofibrinogenaemia (DIC, severe liver disease), hypogammaglobulinaemia, agammaglobulinaemia.
  • Congestive heart failure — venous stasis & low flow.
  • Drugs — high-dose aspirin, corticosteroids, quinine, ACTH, TNF inhibitors.
  • Severe dehydration, shock.
  • Cryoglobulinaemia — at low temperature, plasma gels and RBCs cannot fall.
  • Technical — delayed testing >4 h, tilting tube >3° off vertical, bubbles, clot in sample, short Westergren tube.

Clinical Pearl

Very high ESR (>100 mm/h) should prompt a work-up for multiple myeloma (serum & urine electrophoresis, free light chains), giant-cell arteritis / polymyalgia rheumatica (especially in elderly with headache / shoulder stiffness), or occult malignancy / chronic infection (TB, IE).

Importance of Working in a Health-Care Team

Modern medicine is a team sport — no single professional has the breadth of expertise needed for safe, effective, patient-centred care. The team typically includes doctors, nurses, pharmacists, physiotherapists, dieticians, social workers, lab technicians, radiographers, hospital administrators and the patient's family — each contributing complementary skills.

  • Comprehensive care — combines medical, surgical, psychological, nutritional and social expertise, addressing the whole patient rather than one disease.
  • Reduced medical errors — cross-checks by pharmacists, nurses and second-physician reviewers catch prescribing errors, allergies, drug interactions and wrong-site surgery.
  • Improved outcomes — multidisciplinary stroke units, oncology tumour boards, and cardiac arrest teams have measurable mortality benefits over isolated care.
  • Better communication — structured handovers (SBAR) reduce information loss across shifts.
  • Patient safety — WHO Surgical Safety Checklist, time-outs and team briefing significantly reduce surgical morbidity & mortality.
  • Workload distribution — prevents burnout, ensures continuity of care, enables round-the-clock coverage.
  • Continuity & coordination — avoids duplicate investigations, contradictory plans, and gaps in follow-up.
  • Shared decision-making — patient & family are active partners, improving adherence & satisfaction.
  • Education & mentoring — junior staff learn from seniors; bedside rounds teach clinical reasoning, ethics and procedural skills.
  • Resource optimisation — administrators, microbiologists and infection-control nurses collaborate on antimicrobial stewardship and bed management.
  • Ethical & legal support — ethics committees, hospital lawyers and risk-management teams guide end-of-life decisions, consent, and adverse-event disclosure.

Clinical Pearl

Effective teams share three traits — clear roles, structured communication (closed-loop, SBAR), and psychological safety where any member can voice concerns without fear. The lowest-ranking nurse must be able to halt a surgery — that safety net has prevented countless wrong-site operations.

Indications for Semen Analysis

  • Male infertility workup — primary indication; couple unable to conceive after 12 months (or 6 months if partner >35) of unprotected intercourse.
  • Post-vasectomy confirmation — at 12 & 20 weeks / 20 ejaculations post-procedure to confirm azoospermia.
  • Pre-fertility treatment — IUI, IVF, ICSI; determines need & modality.
  • Assessment after illness / fever / varicocele repair / hormonal therapy.
  • Sperm donor screening — infectious disease, karyotype, sperm function tests.
  • Forensic / sexual assault cases — identification of semen (acid phosphatase, prostate-specific antigen, microscopy for spermatozoa, DNA profiling).
  • Cryopreservation — prior to chemotherapy, radiotherapy, vasectomy, orchiectomy, gender-reassignment.

Microscopic Examination (WHO 5th ed., 2021)

  • Sample collection — by masturbation after 2–7 days abstinence; delivered to lab within 1 h; kept at body temperature. Two samples 7–14 days apart for confirmation.
  • Liquefaction — within 15–30 min at 37°C (proteolytic enzymes from prostate).
  • Macroscopic — volume ≥1.4 mL (lower reference limit); pH ≥7.2; viscosity <2 cm thread; appearance grey-opalescent.
  • Sperm concentration — ≥16 million/mL (lower limit); haemocytometer or computer-assisted semen analysis (CASA).
  • Total sperm number — ≥39 million per ejaculate.
  • Total motility — ≥42% (PR + NP); progressive motility ≥30%.
  • Vitality — ≥54% live (eosin-nigrosin or hypo-osmotic swelling test).
  • Morphology — ≥4% normal forms (strict Kruger criteria); Papanicolaou, Shorr or Diff-Quik stain.
  • Leucocytes — <1 million/mL (peroxidase-positive); pyospermia suggests genital tract infection.
  • Agglutination — significant if >50% sperm agglutinated; suggests anti-sperm antibodies (MAR / IB test).
  • Other cells — immature germ cells, epithelial cells, debris.

Clinical Pearl

One abnormal semen analysis is not infertility — repeat after 12 weeks. Azoospermia with normal testicular volume & FSH suggests obstructive cause (post-infective, CFTR mutation, vasectomy) — surgical sperm retrieval (TESE / PESA) with ICSI can give biological paternity.

Molecular Mechanism of Apoptosis

Apoptosis is executed by a proteolytic cascade of caspases (cysteine-aspartate proteases). Initiator caspases (8, 9, 10) cleave and activate executioner caspases (3, 6, 7), which dismantle the cell.

1. Extrinsic (Death-Receptor) Pathway

  • FasL → Fas (CD95) trimerisation; TNF-α → TNFR1; TRAIL → DR4/5.
  • Receptor recruits adaptor FADD (or TRADD) via death domains.
  • FADD death-effector domain binds procaspase-8 → DISC (death-inducing signalling complex) → auto-activation of caspase-8.
  • Caspase-8 directly cleaves caspase-3, and cleaves Bid to truncated Bid (tBid) which feeds into the intrinsic pathway (cross-talk).

2. Intrinsic (Mitochondrial) Pathway

  • Stimuli: DNA damage, hypoxia, growth-factor withdrawal, ROS, radiation, ER stress, chemotherapy.

Phagocytosis ("cell eating") is the process by which specialised cells — neutrophils, macrophages, monocytes, dendritic cells (and eosinophils to a lesser degree) — internalise particles ≥0.5 µm (microbes, dead cells, debris) into a phagocytic vacuole (phagosome) for destruction and antigen presentation.

  2. Engulfment — pseudopodia zip around the particle (actin polymerisation, Rho-family GTPases Cdc42, Rac). Particle is internalised into a phagosome.

    • Oxygen-dependent (respiratory burst) — NADPH oxidase (phox) reduces O2 to superoxide (O2·−); superoxide dismutase converts to H2O2; myeloperoxidase (MPO) + Cl− → hypochlorous acid (HOCl). Other ROS: hydroxyl radical, singlet oxygen.

    • Nitric oxide — iNOS generates NO·; combined with superoxide → peroxynitrite (ONOO−) — kills mycobacteria, intracellular pathogens.
  5. Exocytosis or antigen presentation — residual debris exocytosed; macrophages/dendritic cells process antigen and present peptide + MHC II to CD4 T-cells, linking innate to adaptive immunity.

Complications in Healing of Skin Wounds

  • Infection — most common; staphylococcal/streptococcal; causes delayed healing, suppuration, cellulitis, abscess, wound dehiscence.
  • Dehiscence — splitting of opposed wound edges; usually day 5–8 before adequate collagen deposition; abdominal wound burst with evisceration is surgical emergency.
  • Incisional hernia — late complication of abdominal wound dehiscence; peritoneal sac protrudes through weakened scar.
  • Hypertrophic scar — raised, red scar confined to wound boundary; common in young, burns, tension areas; often regresses.
  • Keloid — scar extends beyond wound margins, does not regress; familial, dark-skinned individuals; over-production of collagen type III; common on sternum, earlobe, shoulder.
  • Contracture — shortening of scar across joints → deformity & limited motion; classic complication of burns.
  • Implantation (epidermal) cyst — epidermal cells trapped in dermis during closure.
  • Neuroma — traumatic neuroma at cut nerve end; painful.
  • Pigmentary changes — hyper- or hypopigmentation in scar.

Distinguish keloid from hypertrophic scar by the margins: keloid extends beyond the original wound, hypertrophic scar stays within it. Keloids tend to recur after excision — combine surgery with intralesional corticosteroid or silicone sheeting to reduce recurrence.

Wound Healing

Wound healing is the orchestrated, overlapping process by which damaged tissue is restored. Three phases:

1. Inflammation (0–3 days)

  • Haemostasis — vasoconstriction, platelet plug, fibrin clot. Platelets release PDGF, TGF-β, FGF, serotonin, histamine.
  • Acute inflammation — neutrophils (24 h) clear bacteria; monocytes convert to macrophages (48–72 h) — phagocytose debris, secrete cytokines (IL-1, TNF-α) and growth factors (PDGF, TGF-β, VEGF) that initiate repair.

2. Proliferation (3 days – 3 weeks)

  • Angiogenesis — VEGF, FGF drive capillary ingrowth; granulation tissue forms (pink, soft, granular).
  • Fibroblast proliferation & collagen deposition — type III initially, then remodelled to type I; provides tensile strength. Driven by TGF-β, PDGF.
  • Epithelialisation — keratinocytes migrate across wound surface (within 24 h for primary, longer for secondary), driven by EGF, KGF.
  • Wound contraction — myofibroblasts (specialised fibroblasts with α-smooth muscle actin) contract and pull edges together (esp. in secondary union).

3. Remodelling / Maturation (3 weeks – 12 months)

  • Type III collagen is replaced by type I; collagen reorganises along tension lines.
  • Vessels regress — scar becomes pale & avascular.
  • Wound tensile strength reaches ~70–80% of normal skin by 3 months; never reaches 100%.

Pathological Calcification

Abnormal deposition of calcium salts in tissues other than osteoid or teeth. Two types:

Dystrophic Calcification

  • Definition — deposition of calcium in dead, degenerated or necrotic tissue with normal serum calcium & phosphate.
  • Pathogenesis — membrane damage releases phosphate; calcium binds to membrane phospholipids & denatured proteins. Hydroxyapatite crystals form, often with ammonium, magnesium, iron.
  • Examples
    • Caseous necrosis in TB ( Ghon complex), histoplasmosis.
    • Atheromatous plaques, damaged heart valves (calcific AS).
    • Old scars, healed infarcts, hyalinised leiomyomas.
    • Psammoma bodies — papillary thyroid carcinoma, serous ovarian cystadenocarcinoma, meningioma, papillary RCC.
    • Cysts — epidermoid, pilar, hydatid.
    • Dead parasites — schistosoma, guinea worm, cysticercus, echinococcus.
    • Fat necrosis (acute pancreatitis) — soap formation.
  • Microscopy — basophilic, amorphous, granular; H&E blue; von Kossa stain (silver) black.

Metastatic Calcification

  • Definition — deposition of calcium in normal tissue due to hypercalcaemia.
  • Causes of hypercalcaemia
    • Hyperparathyroidism (primary, secondary, tertiary).
    • Malignancy — PTHrP (squamous cell carcinoma, breast, renal), lytic bone metastases (breast, myeloma), multiple myeloma.
    • Vitamin D intoxication, sarcoidosis, milk-alkali syndrome.
    • Bone destruction — Paget disease, immobilisation, prolonged bed rest.
    • Renal failure (secondary hyperparathyroidism).
    • Thyrotoxicosis, thiazides, adrenal insufficiency.
  • Sites — kidney (nephrocalcinosis → renal failure), lungs (diffuse interstitial), stomach (fundic), blood vessels, cornea (band keratopathy), myocardium, alveolar walls.
  • Pathogenesis — Ca × P product >70; alkaline environment favours deposition (gastric fundus, lungs).

Clinical Pearl

Dystrophic calcification can be a helpful diagnostic clue — psammoma bodies in papillary thyroid carcinoma; caseating granulomas calcified in old TB; "egg-shell" calcification in silicotic lymph nodes. Metastatic calcification points to underlying hypercalcaemia — always check serum Ca, P, PTH, vitamin D, albumin, renal function.

Type IV (Cell-Mediated) Hypersensitivity

Delayed-type hypersensitivity (DTH) — T-cell mediated immune response that develops 24–72 h after antigen exposure. No antibody involvement; not transferred by serum but by T lymphocytes.

Mechanisms

  1. CD4+ T helper 1 (Th1) pathway — antigen presented by macrophage/dendritic cell on MHC-II → sensitised Th1 cell releases IFN-γ, IL-2, TNF-β → macrophage activation → epithelioid & giant-cell granuloma formation & tissue injury.
  2. CD8+ cytotoxic T-cell pathway — antigen on MHC-I → CTL directly kills target cell via perforin/granzyme & Fas-FasL.
  3. CD4+ Th17 pathway — IL-17, IL-22 recruits neutrophils; drives chronic inflammation & autoimmunity (psoriasis, IBD).

Role of Cytokines & Prostaglandins in Acute Inflammation

Cytokines

Small proteins secreted by activated macrophages, lymphocytes, endothelium, mast cells. Major ones in acute inflammation:

  • IL-1β, TNF-α — from macrophages; induce endothelial adhesion molecules (ICAM, VCAM, E-selectin); activate neutrophils; cause fever, anorexia, hypotension, acute-phase response (CRP, SAA); cachexia in chronic cases.
  • IL-6 — major stimulator of acute-phase proteins (CRP, fibrinogen, hepcidin) from liver; drives B-cell maturation.
  • Chemokines (IL-8 / CXCL8) — potent neutrophil chemoattractant & activator. Others: MCP-1 (CCL2), MIP-1α (CCL3), RANTES (CCL5), eotaxin (CCL11).
  • IL-12 — drives Th1 differentiation & NK activation.
  • IL-17 (from Th17) — recruits neutrophils via IL-8 induction.
  • IL-10, TGF-β — anti-inflammatory; resolve inflammation, promote repair & scarring.

Prostaglandins & Lipid Mediators

Derived from arachidonic acid released from membrane phospholipids by phospholipase A2.

  • Cyclo-oxygenase (COX) pathway
    • PGE2 — vasodilator, potentiate permeability, fever, pain sensitisation (hyperalgesia).
    • PGI2 (prostacyclin) — vasodilator, inhibits platelet aggregation.
    • TXA2 (thromboxane) — vasoconstrictor, platelet aggregation (platelets).
    • PGD2 — mast cells; vasodilator, chemoattractant.
  • Lipoxygenase (LOX) pathway
    • 5-HPETE → LTA4 → LTB4 (neutrophil chemoattractant & activator).
    • LTC4, LTD4, LTE4 — slow-reacting substance of anaphylaxis (SRS-A); bronchoconstriction, vasoconstriction, increased permeability.
  • Lipoxins (LXA4, LXB4) — generated during resolution; inhibit neutrophil recruitment, promote macrophage clearance of apoptotic cells.
  • Resolvins, protectins, maresins — derived from omega-3 fatty acids; actively terminate inflammation.

Clinical Pearl

NSAIDs (aspirin, ibuprofen) inhibit COX-1 & COX-2, reducing PGE2/PGI2 — relieving fever, pain & inflammation but also impairing gastric mucosal protection & renal perfusion. Steroids inhibit phospholipase A2 (lipocortin) and COX-2 induction, blocking both prostaglandins & leukotrienes — hence more potent anti-inflammatory effect.

Hemoparasites

  • Plasmodium spp. — P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae, P. knowlesi — malaria
  • Babesia microti — babesiosis (USA, Europe)
  • Trypanosoma spp. — T. cruzi (Chagas), T. brucei gambiense / rhodesiense (sleeping sickness)
  • Leishmania spp. — L. donovani (kala-azar), L. tropica (cutaneous), L. braziliensis (mucocutaneous)
  • Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi / timori — microfilariae in blood (lymphatic filariasis)
  • Toxoplasma gondii (tachyzoites in blood)
  • Borrelia spp. — relapsing fever, B. burgdorferi (Lyme)
  • Rickettsia, Orientia, Ehrlichia, Anaplasma — intracellular, on endothelium
  • Bartonella bacilliformis — Oroya fever

Laboratory Diagnosis of Malaria

  1. Microscopy — Gold standard
    • Thick smear — concentration of parasites; sensitivity ~5–10 parasites/μL; species ID difficult.
    • Thin smear — species identification, parasite density (per 200 WBC or 1000 RBC), stage of parasite.
    • Stain — Giemsa, Leishman, JSB, Field's.
    • Reporting — parasitaemia % = (parasitised RBC / total RBC) × 100; >2% or >100,000/μL in falciparum = severe disease.
  2. Rapid Diagnostic Tests (RDT)
    • Immunochromatographic card tests detecting parasite LDH (pLDH), histidine-rich protein 2 (HRP-2 — P. falciparum only), aldolase (pan-malarial).
    • Useful in field; limit — does not quantify parasite load; HRP-2 deletions in some P. falciparum strains.
  3. Molecular — PCR
    • Species-specific 18S rRNA PCR; nested PCR for mixed infections.
    • Detects low parasitaemia; useful for species confirmation & research.
  4. Serology — IFA, ELISA for anti-malarial antibodies; useful for blood donor screening & retrospective diagnosis, not for acute.
  5. Other tests — buffy coat smear, quantitative buffy coat (QBC) fluorescent stain, loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP).
  6. Supportive tests — CBC (anaemia, thrombocytopenia), blood glucose (hypoglycaemia in falciparum), LFT, KFT, ABG (acidosis), urine for haemoglobinuria (blackwater fever), G6PD before primaquine.

Clinical Pearl

In P. falciparum, only ring forms & gametocytes are seen in peripheral smear (trophozoites sequester in deep capillaries). Gametocytes are banana-shaped (crescent). Look for high parasitaemia, double-chromatin ring forms, and absence of schizonts — features that distinguish falciparum from benign malarias.

Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)

Etiology

  • Genetic — HLA-DR2, HLA-DR3; C1q, C2, C4 deficiency; twin concordance ~25% monozygotic vs 2% dizygotic.
  • Hormonal — female : male 9:1; oestrogen enhances B-cell autoimmunity; flares in pregnancy & with OCPs.
  • Environmental triggers — UV light (keratinocyte apoptosis → nuclear antigen exposure); drugs (procainamide, hydralazine, isoniazid, anti-TNF → drug-induced lupus, anti-histone positive); infections (EBV).
  • Immune dysregulation — defective clearance of apoptotic bodies; polyclonal B-cell activation; T-helper bias.

Pathogenesis

Triad: (1) autoantibody production (ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, anti-phospholipid); (2) immune complex formation; (3) tissue deposition (glomeruli, skin, serosa, vessels) → complement activation → inflammation. Type II hypersensitivity causes cytopenias (haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia); type III causes glomerulonephritis, vasculitis, serositis.
